case.title: Storm Night
case.mapCap: Palmetto Springs (a made-up town). The red dashed zone must evacuate (leave to stay safe).
case.hook: It’s June Calloway again. A hurricane is coming to Palmetto Springs tonight. I’ll be at the town’s storm center all night, reading the gauges and taking calls. Stay with me. In the morning, we’ll figure out what the storm changed.
case.question: What did the storm change in Palmetto Springs, and was all of it bad?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: A hurricane brings three dangers: strong wind, heavy rain and storm surge (ocean water pushed onto land).

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: the storm clock
clues.t: Each danger had its own effects: wind knocked down a branch and a power line, rain flooded Elm Street, and storm surge pushed seawater onto Bay Street and into Cypress Slough.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: the morning flyover
clues.t: One real storm changed all three layers: the land (dunes washed away, sand on the road), the ecosystem (woods snapped and bare) and the people (homes and a campground swept away).

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: trace the chain
clues.t: Not every effect was bad: the storm’s rain ended a dry spell and refilled the spring and the water underground. In 2008, Tropical Storm Fay raised Lake Okeechobee more than 2 feet in one week.

solve.title: What did the storm change?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: It only knocked down some trees. Nothing else changed.
options.why: Check Clues 2 and 3. Did the storm change more than trees?

options.t: It changed the land, the ecosystem and the people, and every one of those changes was bad.
options.why: Check Clue 4. What happened to the spring after the storm?

options.t: Its wind, rain and storm surge changed the land, the ecosystem and the people. Most changes were harmful, but its rain also refilled the spring.
options.why: Case cracked! You traced every danger through all three layers, and you found the good side, too. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

bulletin.title: The weather radio
todo: Press Play and listen. You can read along on the paper.
Tap the three DANGERS the storm is bringing. A place or a time is not a danger.
lines: This is a hurricane warning for Palmetto Springs. A strong hurricane will reach the coast tonight.
[[wind|Winds of 100 miles per hour]] can knock down trees and power lines.
[[rain|Heavy rain]], up to 20 inches, can flood streets.
[[surge|Storm surge]], ocean water pushed onto land by the storm, can rise 8 feet near the bay.

Everyone on [[x:Bay Street is a place, not a danger. What could hurt people there?|Bay Street]] must evacuate by [[x:6 PM is a time, not a danger. Look for something the storm brings.|6 PM]]. Go to a safe place inland (away from the coast) now.

dangers.does: knocks down trees and power lines
pushes ocean water onto land near the bay

bulletin.win: Three dangers: wind, rain and storm surge. Each one causes different effects. That’s a clue.

stormclock.afterText: The difference is whether the event can harm
stormclock.title: The storm clock
todo: Press the button to move through the night. Watch the wind, the rain and the tide gauge.
When a call comes in, drag the danger that caused it onto the call (or tap a danger, then the call).

why.t: A tall ruler on the dock that shows how high the bay water is.

stormclock.startLine: It’s 6 PM. Bay Street is empty: those families evacuated. Press the button to move to 8 PM.
stormclock.waitLine: A new call came in! Drag the cause onto it (or tap a cause, then the call).

hours.note: The strongest part of the storm hits.
Still strong. The bay is still high.

hours.quiet: No new calls. The wind is dropping, and the bay is going back down.

hours.note: Sunrise. The storm is moving away.
hours.quiet: Good morning! The storm is moving away. Answer the question below.

notice.head: Evacuation order · 4 PM
notice.t: Everyone in the red zone along Bay Street must leave by 6 PM. The bay could rise up to 8 feet.

calls.t: A big oak branch snapped and fell across the road.

miss.rain: Rain soaks the ground, but what pushes on a branch so hard that it snaps?
miss.surge: Pine Ave is far from the bay. Look at the map. Can seawater reach it?

calls.why: Strong wind pushes hard on branches until they snap.

calls.t: The power is out on the whole street. A power line is down.

miss.rain: Rain alone doesn’t pull down a power line. What could?
miss.surge: Oak Street is far from the bay. Look at the map.

calls.why: The wind blew a tree onto the power line and knocked the power out.

calls.t: Salty water is coming up the street and into the houses!

miss.wind: Wind pushes, but where did all that SALTY water come from? Check the tide gauge.
miss.rain: Rain is fresh water. This water is salty and came from the bay. Check the tide gauge.

calls.why: The tide gauge hit 8 feet. Storm surge pushed the bay onto land. That’s why Bay Street evacuated before the storm.

calls.t: The street is flooded. The storm drains are overflowing.

miss.surge: Elm Street is far from the bay. Look at the map. What else is falling from the sky?
miss.wind: Wind doesn’t fill a street with water. What is falling from the sky?

calls.why: Rain fell faster than the storm drains could carry it away.

calls.t: Salty bay water is pouring into the wetland.

miss.rain: Rain is fresh water. Which danger brings SALTY water?
miss.wind: Wind pushes the water, but which danger IS the water? Check the tide gauge.

calls.why: Storm surge pushed salty bay water into a freshwater wetland. Salt can hurt plants and animals that need fresh water.

stormclock.q: Why did the town tell Bay Street to evacuate, but not Elm Street?

opts.t: Bay Street is next to the bay, where storm surge pushes seawater onto land.
The wind blew only on Bay Street.
opts.miss: Look at the calls. Did the wind hit only Bay Street?
Look at Elm Street’s call. What flooded it?

stormclock.win: Each danger caused different effects in different places. That’s a clue.

flyover.title: The morning flyover
todo: Drag the slider to compare BEFORE and AFTER.
Tap each number on the photo. Then stamp it: Land, Ecosystem or People.

why.t: Mexico Beach, a real Florida town. Hurricane Michael hit it in October 2018. The next day, a plane took the “after” photo of the same spot.

before.label: BEFORE · April 2017
before.alt: From the air: a beach town with a campground full of RVs, houses among green woods, a pond and creek, and a road beside a wide white beach.

after.label: AFTER · Oct. 11, 2018
after.alt: The same town the day after Hurricane Michael: the campground is bare sand, many houses are gone, the trees are brown and broken, and sand covers the road by the beach.

flyover.credit: Mexico Beach, Florida, in April 2017 and on October 11, 2018, the day after Hurricane Michael: NOAA aerial photos, shared by the USGS Coastal Change Hazards team, via Wikimedia Commons
flyover.startLine: Tap a number on the photo.
flyover.askLine: Which layer is this? Stamp it below.

spots.label: The woods
spots.t: Before: thick green woods where birds and other animals lived. After: the trees are snapped and bare, so those animals lost their homes and food.

miss.land: Fallen trees change the land, too. But think about the animals that lived here. Which layer is about living things?
miss.people: No one lives in these woods. Who lost a home here?

spots.label: The campground
spots.t: Before: a campground full of RVs and cabins where families stayed. After: almost all of it was swept away. Only bare sand is left.

miss.land: The sand is land, but what did PEOPLE lose here?
miss.eco: RVs and cabins belong to people. Which layer is that?

spots.label: The pond and creek
spots.t: Before: green woods grew all around the water. After: the edges are torn up and full of mud, sand and broken trees. Fish, turtles and birds live in places like this.

miss.land: Look at what lives in and around the water. Which layer is that?
miss.people: Is this about people’s homes, or about the plants and animals?

spots.label: The beach road
spots.t: Before: a road beside a wide white beach with sand dunes. After: waves and storm surge washed the dunes away and spread beach sand across the road.

miss.eco: Sand and dunes aren’t alive. Which layer is about the ground itself?
miss.people: The road is for people, but what changed here: the sand and the dunes. Which layer is that?

spots.label: Homes by the beach
spots.t: Many homes are gone. A few right next to them are still standing. Why? You’ll find out next lesson.

miss.land: Homes belong to people. Which layer is that?
miss.eco: Homes belong to people. Which layer is that?

opts.t: The storm changed only the people layer.
opts.miss: Look at your stamps. Did you use only 🏠?

opts.t: One storm changed the land, the ecosystem AND the people.
The storm changed only the beach.
opts.miss: Look at your stamps. What happened to the woods and the homes?

flyover.win: One storm changed all three layers. That’s a clue.

stormchain.title: Trace the chain
todo: This chain follows the storm surge. Drag each card into its box (or tap a card, then a box).
Two cards don’t fit: they came from a different danger.

why.t: One cause leads to an effect, and that effect leads to the next one, like falling dominoes.

links: with the dunes gone, seawater rushed in
and flooded the street by the bay

cards.t: Storm surge: the bay rose to 8 feet

missSlot.land: This is what STARTED it all. Which box comes first?
missSlot.eco: This is what STARTED it all. Which box comes first?
missSlot.people: This is what STARTED it all. Which box comes first?

cards.t: Waves washed sand off the beach and over the dunes
cards.miss: Sand and dunes aren’t alive, and they aren’t people. Which box is about the ground?

cards.t: Salty bay water poured into Cypress Slough, a freshwater wetland
cards.miss: A wetland is full of plants and animals. Which box is that?

cards.t: Bay Street homes flooded, but the families had evacuated and were safe
cards.miss: Homes and families are people. Which box is that?

cards.t: The power went out on Oak Street
cards.miss: That effect came from the WIND, not the storm surge. Follow the seawater.
That came from the RAIN, far from the bay. This chain follows the storm surge.

stormchain.doneLine: The chain is complete: one cause, three layers.

twist.btn: 🌅 One week later: June’s last reading
twist.head: Palmetto Spring · one week after the storm
rows: Two months with almost no rain. The spring was low, and the town asked everyone to save water.
The water in the town well is 3 feet higher. The spring is flowing strong again.
twist.t: The storm’s 20 inches of rain soaked into the ground and refilled the water stored in the rock underground.

stormchain.q: Was every effect of the storm bad?

opts.t: Yes. Every effect of a hurricane is bad.
opts.miss: Look at June’s last reading. What happened to the spring?

opts.t: No. Its rain ended a dry spell and refilled the water underground.
No. The storm surge helped the wetland.
opts.miss: Salty water hurts a freshwater wetland. Look at the spring instead.

stormchain.fact: This happens in real life, too. In August 2008, Tropical Storm Fay dropped heavy rain on Florida after one of its driest times on record. Lake Okeechobee rose more than 2 feet in one week.
stormchain.win: A natural event can harm AND help. That’s your last clue.

tool.name: Rain gauge
tool.teaser: Read the rain gauge after each part of the storm and add up all the rain.
tool.done: You read the rain gauge like a weather watcher. A rain gauge sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.t: A clear tube with inch marks that catches rain, so you can measure exactly how much fell. Volunteers all over Florida read one every morning and share the numbers with weather scientists.

raingauge.title: How much rain did the storm drop?
todo: Tap each part of the gauge to learn it.
Check the gauge after each part of the storm, and read how many inches fell.
raingauge.readQ: Read the gauge. How many inches of rain?
raingauge.emptyLine: You wrote it down and emptied the gauge.

parts.label: The funnel
parts.t: It catches the rain and pours it into the tube, so none splashes out.

parts.label: The tube
parts.t: Its marks are inches, like a ruler standing up. The top of the water shows how much rain fell.

parts.label: Where it goes
parts.t: On a post in an open spot, away from trees and roofs, so nothing blocks the rain or drips extra water in.

periods.note: The rain got heavier as the storm came closer.
The heaviest rain fell while the storm was right over town.
The storm was moving away, but its rain bands kept coming.
The last rain bands passed. The sun came out at sunset.

q.q: How much rain fell in the whole storm?

opts.why: That’s the most in one part. Add all four parts together.
Right! 4.5 + 6.5 + 5 + 4 = 20 inches. Florida gets about 54 inches of rain in a whole year, so this one storm dropped more than a third of a year’s rain in one day.
That’s just the last part. Add all four parts together.

q1.A: If they were the same, we wouldn’t need two words. Which one makes something happen?
q1.C: Nature can be a cause, and people can feel effects, but that isn’t what the words mean. Which answer says what each word does?

q2.B: Closed roads change people’s day. Which layer is that?
q2.C: A house belongs to people. Which answer is about animals and plants?

q3.A: Hurricanes form over warm ocean water, not under the ground. Which event starts with rock dissolving?
q3.B: Wildfires need dry plants and a spark. Which event starts with rock dissolving?

cer-4.label: your reasoning
cer-4.re: because|so |this shows|that shows|this means|that means|which means|proves|since

ans-2: What does a fire clear away in a pine forest?
Some pine cones and plants need fire. Now, why could the same fire be dangerous for people?
Try: A wildfire can help the ecosystem because ___. But it can harm people because ___.
ans-3: Think about the flyover photos. Did the storm change only one layer?
Pick one storm effect and follow it into another layer, like the dunes and the wetland.
Try: It is important to trace all three layers because ___. For example, ___.
cer-4: First decide: is EVERY natural event a disaster?
Think about June’s last reading at the spring, and about wildfires in pine forests.
Try: I ___ because ___. One piece of evidence is ___. Another is ___.

planner.title: Your claim and two pieces of evidence

rows.label: 2. Pick two pieces of evidence from the lesson
options: The storm’s surge flooded Bay Street homes and pushed salty water into Cypress Slough.
The storm’s rain ended a dry spell and refilled the spring and the water underground.
Some Florida pine forests need fire to clear out low bushes and release their seeds.
A summer thunderstorm is a natural event, but it is normal weather, not a hazard.

planner.note: Tap your side and two facts. Then write your reasoning in your own words.

welcome.label: Welcome · storm night
welcome.script: Hi, it’s June. Tonight a hurricane is heading straight for Palmetto Springs. I’m at the town’s storm center, and I’ll stay up all night reading the gauges and answering calls. Look at the map in the case file. See the red zone by the bay? Those families have to leave by six o’clock. Stay with me tonight. In the morning, we’ll figure out what the storm changed.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · the weather radio (Clue 1)
warmup.script: My weather radio just went off. Press Play and listen closely. Then tap the three dangers the storm is bringing. Careful: a place or a time is not a danger. After that, write three things you think this storm might change in our town.

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Act out “evacuate” by grabbing a bag and walking off screen; point “cause” and “effect” with two hands like a domino push.

part1.label: Part 1 · the storm clock (Clue 2)
part1.script: Here’s the storm clock. Press the button to move through the night, two hours at a time. Watch the wind, the rain and the tide gauge on the dock. When a call comes in, drag the danger that caused it onto the call. Then you can move to the next hour.

part2.label: Part 2 · the morning flyover (Clue 3)
part2.script: Palmetto Springs is made up, but these photos are real. They show Mexico Beach, Florida, before and after Hurricane Michael. Drag the slider to compare. Then tap each number and stamp it: land, ecosystem or people.

explore.label: Part 4 · trace the chain (Clue 4)
explore.script: Good morning! The storm is gone, and the night’s evidence is on my table. Let’s follow the storm surge, one link at a time: the cause, the land, the ecosystem, then the people. Two cards came from a different danger, so leave them out. When you finish, I have one more reading to show you.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab: what did the storm change, and was all of it bad? Then answer two questions, trace a chain for any Florida natural event in Part C, and write your CER. Your answers save as you type.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says all natural events are disasters, and the fewer the better. Hmm. Think about last night’s storm. Then think about my last reading at the spring. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease 17.02 (design ways to keep a town safer, like an engineer).
closing.script: Case closed! You followed a hurricane through a whole night, and you traced its effects on the land, the ecosystem and the people. You even found the good side. Next time, we’ll think like engineers and design ways to keep a town like ours safer before the next storm.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how a natural event changes the land, the ecosystem and the people?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: Storm surge pushed salty bay water onto Bay Street and into the wetland.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “storm surge”, “Bay Street” and “wetland”. Those words tell the cause and where its effects landed. Small words like “and” and “the” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
